drafts.title: Reduce harsh ride on broken pavement so bumps feel less jarring
drafts.description: When driving over broken pavement or poor-quality roads customers feel fewer and smaller jolts; occupants perceive improved comfort without noticeably degrading handling.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On a standardized broken-pavement track at 40 mph (64 km/h) the vertical seat acceleration RMS at the driver seat shall be ≤ 1.2 m/s² and test-driver subjective comfort (100‑point scale) shall improve by ≥ 10 points versus the current 5 Series baseline.
assumptions: Current 5 Series baseline metrics are available for comparison at development start.
Improvements may combine suspension tuning, damping control and software; these are deliverable within successor vehicle development cycle.
uncertainties: Improvements on very rough roads may trade off with sporty handling preferences for some customers.
Exact test-track profile selection affects measured RMS values; use agreed industry-standard profile.

drafts.title: Provide a clearly improved real-world single-charge/-tank range for long‑range variant
drafts.description: Customers can reliably drive long distances without range anxiety; the long‑range variant delivers a verified, real-world range that meets long-distance driving expectations.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: The long-range variant shall demonstrate a verified real-world driving range of ≥ 400 miles (≥ 645 km) on a combined EPA-equivalent test route (mixed city/highway) under typical driving conditions.
assumptions: Successor can offer a long-range battery/powertrain variant within packaging and weight constraints.
EPA-equivalent mixed driving test is an acceptable industry measure for 'real-world' range comparison at launch.
uncertainties: Customer requests for 600–700 miles exceed what is realistic within 3–5 years for this vehicle class; reaching 400 miles depends on battery energy density, efficiency and allowable pack size.
Real-world range will vary with temperature, load and driving style; marketing must communicate expected conditions.

drafts.title: Make it easy to find compatible fast chargers during trips
drafts.description: When planning or driving a long trip the car shows compatible high-speed chargers along the route with clear compatibility and estimated charging time so customers can plan stops quickly and confidently.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: For 90% of multi-stop routes ≥ 200 miles, the route planner shall propose at least one compatible fast charger within ±10 miles of the optimal route; compatibility indicator and estimated plug/adapter requirement and estimated charge time shall be shown. For at least 70% of proposed stops the planner shall present live availability or last-known status.
assumptions: Access to third‑party charger network APIs and roaming/roaming-data agreements are available during development.
Vehicle knows its supported charging connectors and adapters.
uncertainties: Third-party network data availability and quality vary by region and operator.
Live availability coverage may be lower in less-populated areas.

drafts.title: Show charge port status at a glance from outside the car
drafts.description: Customers can tell whether the vehicle is charging, fully charged, or has a charging fault without opening an app or looking at the instrument cluster — by glancing at the charge port indicator.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Charge-port indicator shall present three unambiguous visible states (charging, complete, fault) readable from 3 meters in daylight and at night; while charging, estimated time to full shall be displayed in the vehicle UI within ±10 minutes accuracy.
assumptions: SOC and time-to-full estimates are available from the vehicle management system with the stated accuracy under normal conditions.
Indicator location visible when vehicle is parked at typical charging positions.
uncertainties: Visibility can be affected by severe glare or unusual charger orientations.
Time‑to‑full accuracy degrades at very low or very high ambient temperatures.

drafts.title: Reduce distracting wind noise at highway speeds
drafts.description: When driving at highway speeds customers do not experience wind noise that distracts conversation or audio content.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: At 75 mph (120 km/h) on a smooth highway with crosswind up to 10 mph (16 km/h), cabin A‑weighted SPL at the driver ear shall be ≤ 68 dB(A). In in‑vehicle subjective tests the annoyance score must be reduced by ≥ 20% versus the current 5 Series.
assumptions: Measurement position is standardized (driver ear, microphone position per SAE standard).
Comparisons use the current 5 Series baseline tested on the same route/conditions.
uncertainties: Wind-noise performance depends on door seals, mirror design and window fit; changes in one area may affect others.
Crosswind and vehicle speed variations can cause measurement variability.

drafts.title: Lane-keeping assist steers smoothly and predictably in curves
drafts.description: When lane-keeping assist is active on highways and marked curves the system provides steady, predictable steering without abrupt corrections that feel nervous to the driver.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On marked freeway curves at speeds up to 70 mph (113 km/h) with standard lane markings, active lane-keeping shall produce lateral position changes ≤ 0.5 m over any 3-second window and lateral jerk ≤ 0.5 m/s³; driver-reported abrupt-steer events shall be ≤ 1 per 1000 miles in fleet validation.
assumptions: Lane markings are present and within typical reflectivity standards.
Fleet validation uses a representative sample of road geometries and speeds.
uncertainties: Performance may degrade on faded or missing lane markings or in adverse weather.
Trade-offs exist between tight lane-centering and perceived naturalness; tuning will reflect UX priorities.
